# Large datasets

## Exercise 9.1 {-}

For the S2 image (above), find out in which order the bands are
using `st_get_dimension_values()`, and try to find out (e.g. by internet
search) which spectral bands / colors they correspond to.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
f = "sentinel/S2A_MSIL1C_20180220T105051_N0206_R051_T32ULE_20180221T134037.zip"
  granule = system.file(file = f, package = "starsdata")
file.size(granule)
base_name = strsplit(basename(granule), ".zip")[[1]]
s2 = paste0("SENTINEL2_L1C:/vsizip/", granule, "/", base_name, 
	".SAFE/MTD_MSIL1C.xml:10m:EPSG_32632")
library(stars)
(p = read_stars(s2, proxy = TRUE))
st_get_dimension_values(p, "band")
```

## Python

```{python}
import glob, os, tempfile, time
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import geopandas as gpd
import shapely
import rasterio
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from rasterio.enums import Resampling
from rasterio.features import geometry_mask
from rasterio.windows import from_bounds

# the starsdata package must be installed in R for this file to be found
f = "sentinel/S2A_MSIL1C_20180220T105051_N0206_R051_T32ULE_20180221T134037.zip"
granule = sorted(glob.glob(os.path.expanduser(f"~/R/*/*/starsdata/{f}")))[-1]
print(round(os.path.getsize(granule)))
base_name = os.path.basename(granule).replace(".zip", "")
s2 = (f"SENTINEL2_L1C:/vsizip/{granule}/{base_name}"
      ".SAFE/MTD_MSIL1C.xml:10m:EPSG_32632")

src = rasterio.open(s2)  # opens the file, does not read the pixel values
print(src.shape, src.count, src.crs)
extent = (src.bounds.left, src.bounds.right, src.bounds.bottom, src.bounds.top)
print(src.descriptions)  # band order: B4 (red), B3 (green), B2 (blue), B8 (near infrared)
```
:::

## Exercise 9.2 {-}

Compute NDVI for the S2 image, using `st_apply` and an an appropriate 
`ndvi` function.  Plot the result to screen, and then write the
result to a GeoTIFF. Explain the difference in runtime between
plotting and writing.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
ndvi_fn = function(r, g, b, nir) (nir-r)/(nir+r)
ndvi = st_apply(p, 1:2, ndvi_fn)
plot(ndvi)
```

## Python

```{python}
def read_down(factor):
    """read the image downsampled by `factor`: every (factor+1)-th pixel"""
    n = int(np.ceil(src.width / (factor + 1)))
    x = src.read(out_shape=(src.count, n, n), resampling=Resampling.nearest)
    tr = src.transform * src.transform.scale(src.width / n, src.height / n)
    return x.astype("float64"), tr

p1, tr1 = read_down(30)

def ndvi_fn(r, g, b, nir):
    return (nir - r) / (nir + r)

ndvi_down = ndvi_fn(*p1)  # computed on the downsampled image only
plt.imshow(ndvi_down, extent=extent)
plt.colorbar()
plt.show()
```
:::

Alternatively, one could use

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
ndvi_slow = function(x) (x[4]-x[1])/(x[4]+x[1])
```

## Python

```{python}
def ndvi_slow(x):  # x has the four band values of a single pixel
    return (x[3] - x[0]) / (x[3] + x[0])

# apply it to every pixel of the (small) downsampled image: much slower
# than the vectorised function above
ndvi_s = np.apply_along_axis(ndvi_slow, 0, p1)
np.allclose(ndvi_s, ndvi_down, equal_nan=True)
```
:::

but that is much less efficient (called for every pixel, rather than chunked). 

Write to a tiff:

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
system.time(write_stars(ndvi, "ndvi.tif"))
```

## Python

```{python}
out = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "ndvi.tif")
profile = src.profile | dict(driver="GTiff", count=1, dtype="float32", nodata=np.nan,
                             compress="deflate", tiled=True, blockxsize=256, blockysize=256)
profile.pop("photometric", None)

t0 = time.time()
with rasterio.open(out, "w", **profile) as dst:
    for _, w in dst.block_windows(1):  # process the full image in blocks
        r, nir = (src.read(i, window=w).astype("float32") for i in (1, 4))
        with np.errstate(invalid="ignore", divide="ignore"):
            dst.write(((nir - r) / (nir + r)).astype("float32"), 1, window=w)
print("seconds:", round(time.time() - t0, 1))
```
:::

The runtime difference is caused by the fact that `plot` downsamples,
so computes a very small fraction of the available pixels, where
`write_stars` computes all pixels, and then writes them, at full (original) resolution.

## Exercise 9.3 {-}

Plot an RGB composite of the S2 image, using the `rgb` argument
to `plot()`, and then by using `st_rgb()` first.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
plot(p, rgb = 1:3)
# plot(st_rgb(p[,,,1:3], maxColorValue=13600)) # FIXME: fails
```

## Python

```{python}
# red, green, blue are bands 1:3 (B4, B3, B2); stretch to the 2-98% range
rgb = np.moveaxis(p1[:3], 0, -1)
lo, hi = np.nanpercentile(rgb, [2, 98])
plt.imshow(np.clip((rgb - lo) / (hi - lo), 0, 1), extent=extent)
plt.show()
```
:::

## Exercise 9.4 {-}

select five random points from the bounding box of `S2`, and extract
the band values at these points. What is the class of the object returned?
Convert the object returned to an `sf` object.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
pts =  p |> st_bbox() |> st_as_sfc() |> st_sample(5)
(p5 = st_extract(p, pts))
class(p5)
st_as_sf(p5)
```

## Python

```{python}
rng = np.random.default_rng(4821)
xy = np.column_stack([rng.uniform(extent[0], extent[1], 5),
                      rng.uniform(extent[2], extent[3], 5)])
p5 = pd.DataFrame(list(src.sample(xy)), columns=["B4", "B3", "B2", "B8"])
p5["x"], p5["y"] = xy[:, 0], xy[:, 1]
print(type(p5))  # a pandas DataFrame
gpd.GeoDataFrame(p5, geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(p5.x, p5.y), crs=src.crs)
```
:::

## Exercise 9.5 {-}

For the 10 km radius circle around `POINT(390000  5940000)`, compute
the mean pixel values of the S2 image when downsampling the images
with factor 30, and on the original resolution. Compute the relative
difference between the results.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
b = st_buffer(st_sfc(st_point(c(390000, 5940000)), crs = st_crs(p)), 
	units::set_units(10, km))
plot(p[,,,1], reset = FALSE, axes = TRUE)
plot(b, col = NA, border = 'green', add = TRUE)
p1 = st_as_stars(p, downsample = 30)
a1 = aggregate(p1, b, mean)
```

## Python

```{python}
b = shapely.Point(390000, 5940000).buffer(10000, quad_segs=60)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.imshow(p1[0], extent=extent, cmap="gray")
ax.plot(*b.exterior.xy, color="green")
plt.show()

p1, tr1 = read_down(30)
mask1 = geometry_mask([b], out_shape=p1.shape[1:], transform=tr1, invert=True)
a1 = p1[:, mask1].mean(axis=1)
a1
```
:::

For the full resolution, this takes a while:

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r eval=TRUE}
system.time(a2 <- aggregate(p, b, mean))
```

## Python

```{python}
t0 = time.time()
win = from_bounds(*b.bounds, transform=src.transform).round_offsets().round_lengths()
full = src.read(window=win).astype("float64")  # only the part covering the circle
mask2 = geometry_mask([b], out_shape=full.shape[1:],
                      transform=src.window_transform(win), invert=True)
a2 = full[:, mask2].mean(axis=1)
print("seconds:", round(time.time() - t0, 1))
a2
```
:::

Relative differences: we will work on the array of the stars objects:

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
(a1[[1]] - a2[[1]])/((a1[[1]]+a2[[1]])/2)
```

## Python

```{python}
(a1 - a2) / ((a1 + a2) / 2)
```
:::

Alternatively one could convert `a1` and `a2` to a `data.frame`, using
`as.data.frame`, and work on the third column of the data frames.

## Exercise 9.6  {-}

Use `hist` to compute the histogram on the downsampled S2 image.
Also do this for each of the bands. Use `ggplot2` to compute a
single plot with all four histograms in facets.

```{r echo=FALSE}
dev.off() # in case of source'ing raw R script
```

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
hist(p1)
hist(p1[,,,1])
hist(p1[,,,2])
hist(p1[,,,3])
hist(p1[,,,4])
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(as.data.frame(p1), aes(x = EPSG_32632)) +
		geom_histogram() + facet_wrap(~band)
```

## Python

```{python}
from plotnine import ggplot, aes, geom_histogram, facet_wrap

names = ["B4", "B3", "B2", "B8"]
plt.hist(p1.ravel(), bins=30)  # all bands
plt.show()
for name, band in zip(names, p1):
    plt.hist(band.ravel(), bins=30)
    plt.title(name)
    plt.show()

df = pd.DataFrame({"band": np.repeat(names, p1[0].size), "value": p1.ravel()})
(
    ggplot(df, aes(x="value"))
    + geom_histogram(bins=30)
    + facet_wrap("band")
).show()
```
:::

## Exercise 9.7 {-}

Use `st_crop` to crop the S2 image to the area covered by the 10 km circle.
Plot the results. Explore the effect of setting argument `crop = FALSE`

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
plot(st_crop(p, b))
plot(st_crop(p, b, crop = FALSE))
```

## Python

```{python}
# work on the downsampled image, as plot() does
x0, y0 = tr1.c, tr1.f
inside = geometry_mask([b], out_shape=p1.shape[1:], transform=tr1, invert=True)

# crop = TRUE: restrict to the bounding box of the circle, mask the rest
rows, cols = np.where(inside)
r0, r1, c0, c1 = rows.min(), rows.max() + 1, cols.min(), cols.max() + 1
cropped = np.where(inside, p1[0], np.nan)[r0:r1, c0:c1]
ext = (x0 + c0 * tr1.a, x0 + c1 * tr1.a, y0 + r1 * tr1.e, y0 + r0 * tr1.e)
plt.imshow(cropped, extent=ext)
plt.show()

# crop = FALSE: mask the pixels outside the circle, but keep the full extent
plt.imshow(np.where(inside, p1[0], np.nan),
           extent=extent)
plt.show()
```
:::

## Exercise 9.8 {-}

With the downsampled image, compute the logical layer where all four
bands have pixel values higher than 1000. Use a raster algebra expression
on the four bands (use `split` first), or use `st_apply` for this.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
p_spl = split(p1)
p_spl$high = p_spl$B4 > 1000 & p_spl$B3 > 1000 & p_spl$B2 > 1000 & p_spl$B8 > 1000
plot(p_spl["high"])
```

## Python

```{python}
p_spl = dict(zip(["B4", "B3", "B2", "B8"], p1))  # one array per band
p_spl["high"] = ((p_spl["B4"] > 1000) & (p_spl["B3"] > 1000) &
                 (p_spl["B2"] > 1000) & (p_spl["B8"] > 1000))
plt.imshow(p_spl["high"], extent=extent)
plt.show()
```
:::

alternative, using `st_apply` on the band dimension

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
p2 = st_apply(p1, 1:2, function(x) all(x > 1000))
plot(p2)
```

## Python

```{python}
p2 = np.all(p1 > 1000, axis=0)  # reduce over the band dimension
plt.imshow(p2, extent=extent)
plt.show()
```
:::
